entries.claim: The Catechism explains Christ as the Greek rendering of the Hebrew messianic title and its meaning of anointing.

The Catechism explains the salvation meaning of the name Jesus with reference to Matthew 1:21. This supports the theological explanation, not the complete Latin paradigm or every historical etymological reconstruction.
The singular paradigm gives Jesus in the nominative, Jesum in the accusative and Jesu in the four remaining cases.
The name Abel is recorded both as indeclinable and with inflected variants.
The feminine noun Pentecoste has the genitive Pentecostes and denotes the fiftieth day after Easter.
The senses range from releasing a person or acquitting a defendant to bringing work to completion.
The verb belongs to the second conjugation and has the infinitive ending -ēre.
The fourth-declension noun can denote an action, an act of a play, a right of passage for cattle, or a Roman land measure.
Aedificatio denotes building and, figuratively, instruction or edification.
The deponent aemulor can mean to emulate someone or to envy them.
The principal parts include attuli and allātum. The infinitive is afferre.
Amen can confirm what has just been said or introduce a solemn statement in biblical Latin.
Appareo is intransitive in the sense of coming into view or becoming visible.
Appendo can mean to hang something up or to weigh it.
Attendo can mean to give heed or direct one's attention to something.
The adjective augustus can describe something majestic, venerable, or worthy of honour.
Beatitudo denotes happiness or blessedness as a state.
Calamus names a reed and, by extension, a writing pen made from one.
Cano can describe the sounding of an instrument. The entry gives trumpets among its examples.
Carmen can denote a song or poem. Dicere carmen is among the expressions cited.
Cathedra denotes a chair and, in particular contexts, a teacher’s or bishop’s seat.
Cautio denotes care or precaution. In legal usage it can designate a guarantee given orally or in writing.
The senses include the string of a musical instrument and a rope or cord.
Chorus can denote a dance or the company of people who dance and sing.
The entry illustrates clangor, a ringing or resounding noise, with the sound of trumpets.
Coaeternus is an ecclesiastical Latin adjective meaning coeternal.
Collegium can denote a body of people who share an office or occupation.
Colloco can take in with the ablative to specify where something is placed.
The senses include a pillar or column, a figurative support, and a column of cloud.
Alongside trade, commercium can denote exchange, communication, or fellowship.
The first entry treats comparing, matching or pairing things.
The second entry treats preparing, collecting or procuring something.
Concilio can mean to unite people, win someone over, or procure something.
Concilium can denote an assembly, a deliberative council, or a bond of union.
Concludo can mean to enclose, bring to an end, or draw an inference.
Congero describes bringing things together. Its uses include heaping up, building, and compiling.
The deponent consequor can mean to follow, reach, or obtain.
Consisto ranges from taking a stand or halting to remaining or consisting in something.
As a substantive, consors can denote a partner or someone who shares in something.
Constituo can mean to set in place, establish, appoint, or determine.
The noun is derived from constituo and can denote a disposition, order, or arrangement.
Consto can describe things standing together or continuing in being.
Consuetudo denotes habit or custom and can also describe familiarity or association.
Continentia can mean restraint of the passions, temperance, or moderation.
Contineo can mean to hold together, contain, keep fast, or restrain.
Contraho can describe gathering things together, entering an agreement, or incurring guilt.
Contrarius means opposite or opposed and can also mean hostile. E contrario introduces the converse.
The recorded senses include frequent use, residence, and association with others.
Corona can designate a wreath, a crown, or a reward, including the crown of martyrdom.
Corrumpo can mean to ruin, spoil, corrupt, bribe, or falsify.
Credere can take a personal dative. Ecclesiastical examples also use in with the accusative for putting one's faith in someone.
The entry gives crepito, crepitare for making a repeated rattling, crackling, or rustling sound.
The fourth-declension noun covers cultivation, care, worship, and manner of dress.
Cura can express care or anxiety, responsibility for something, or the care of a patient.
Curatio includes care or management and, in a medical context, treatment.
Cursus can designate a course or passage, including the passage of time.
The instrument is described as two hollow metal plates that ring when struck together.
Defensio can mean the act of defending someone, including a defence presented in speech or writing.
Defero can mean to carry something to someone, confer an honour, or report a matter.
Delectatio ordinarily denotes delight, enjoyment, or pleasure.
The figurative senses of devoro include suppressing something or enduring it, alongside the literal sense of swallowing.
Dexter denotes the right-hand side and also has figurative senses of skill and good fortune. Both dextera and dextra occur.
Diffamo can describe spreading a report, publicly proclaiming something, or maligning a person.
The principal parts distinguish the present stem fund- from the perfect fūd- and supine fūs-.
The deponent dignor can take an infinitive in the sense of deigning to do something.
The genitive dolōris has a long penultimate vowel.
The adjective dolōrōsus describes what is painful or full of sorrow.
The deponent dominor can mean to rule or exercise dominion and occurs with a dative complement.
Ecce can introduce a nominative expression or a clause. The entry also records independent accusatives.
The verb edo with the perfect edidi and the supine editum can mean to bring forth.
The fourth-declension noun can designate the result or effect of an action.
Eructo can describe pouring forth an utterance. The entry cites Psalm 44.
The principal parts include ēvādo, ēvāsi, and ēvāsum. A common sense is to escape.
Exsisto, also spelled existo, can mean to emerge, arise, come to be, or exist.
The opening of facio gives fio, factus, and fieri as its passive forms.
Felix has the genitive felīcis. Its senses include favourable, fortunate, and fruitful.
The noun for a fig tree or its fruit has forms of the second and fourth declensions.
Fideliter is treated under fidelis and can mean faithfully or reliably.
The entry gives fīlĭa, ae, with a short i in the syllable before the ending.
The entry fio refers to facio, where its passive forms fio, factus, and fieri are set out.
Floreo is a second-conjugation verb with the infinitive florēre and the perfect florui.
Forma can denote appearance or beauty as well as a pattern, model, or mould.
The verb formido, formidare means to fear or dread and can be used without an expressed object.
The ordinary meanings include race, nation, or people. Ecclesiastical Latin also uses gentes for the Gentiles.
The neuter noun genus, generis can denote descent, a race, a kind, or a class.
Gigno can mean to bear a child as well as to beget one. Examples include a mother as the subject.
Gladius ordinarily denotes a sword and can denote death or killing by extension.
Grandis can describe something large or important, as well as someone full-grown.
The demonstrative hic, haec, hoc can point to a nearby or present person or thing.
The adverb hīc means here, with extensions to the present time or situation.
The fourth-declension noun ictus can designate a blow, stroke, thrust, or beat.
Idoneus can describe someone capable or something suitable or sufficient for a purpose.
Immortalitas denotes exemption from death or imperishability. Its genitive is immortalitātis.
The verb immūto, immūtāre means to change or transform.
Imus is a superlative of inferus. The substantive neuter plural can refer to things below.
With a temporal accusative, in can express duration. In aeternum is one example.
Inaestimabilis can mean impossible to appraise, inestimable, or invaluable.
Incorruptio, genitive incorruptiōnis, denotes incorruptibility or imperishability.
Incorruptus means unspoiled or uncorrupted. The penultimate syllable ends in a consonant.
Induo can describe putting on clothing and, figuratively, taking something upon oneself.
The adjective innumerus means innumerable or beyond counting.
The entry gives inspicio, inspexi, inspectum and senses of examining closely or considering.
Instantia can express pressure, urgency, or persistence.
Intendo can mean to stretch or direct, to exert oneself, or to attend closely to something.
Interventus can denote intervening or coming between, including mediation or assistance.
The adjective invisibilis has the neuter invisibile and means invisible or unseen.
The demonstrative has the three nominative forms is, ea, and id and can serve as a personal pronoun.
Iste can point to something associated with the person addressed.
Both members of the compound meaning oath decline. The entry gives the genitive jurisjurandi.
The present participle of lacteo can denote a nursing child.
Alongside the act of staying, mansio denotes a dwelling. The entry cites two passages in John 14.
Mansuetudo has a long ū in the nominative and can mean gentleness or mildness.
The first-person pronoun ego has the form me in the accusative and ablative.
Ipse can emphasize a personal pronoun and can agree with the subject or the object.
The substantive meritum, treated under mereo, can denote a meritorious deed or the recompense it deserves.
Ministerium can denote attendance, service, ministry, or the duties of an office.
Momentum can denote an instant of time. The entry includes the expression in momento.
Multiplico is a first-conjugation verb meaning to multiply or increase.
The fourth-declension noun nexus denotes binding or a bond and can describe figurative restraints.
The verb of necessity is impersonal. The entry gives oportet and the perfect oportuit.
Opus can mean a work or deed. In opus est it expresses need.
Orbis can denote a circle. Orbis terrarum and orbis terrae are established expressions for the world.
Organum denotes an instrument and can refer to a musical pipe or organ.
Parabola can denote a comparison or a narrative parable.
Pertranseo means to go or pass through. The entry gives the perfect in -īvi and the infinitive in -īre.
The entry refers to praeconius, where the neuter noun includes public proclamation and praise.
The entry gives masculine propheta and prophetes, with the genitive ending -ae.
Prophetīa can mean prophecy or prediction. The entry marks the i before the ending as long.
The adverb prospere occurs under prosper and is illustrated with procedere.
Proximus is the superlative treated under propior. As a noun it can refer to a neighbour or someone close.
Psalterium, genitive psalterii, denotes a stringed instrument and can also designate the Book of Psalms.
Pulchritūdo has a long ū in the nominative and denotes beauty.
The indefinite pronoun can refer to anyone or anything. The neuter forms include quicquam and quidquam.
The additive quoque means also or too and follows the word it emphasizes.
Recenseo can mean to count, review, or go over something in thought.
Recolo can mean to call something to mind or to commemorate it.
Reconcilio can take an accusative for what is reconciled and a dative for the other party.
Reddo includes restoring something as well as giving it back.
Alongside an age or generation, saeculum can denote the world. In saecula saeculorum expresses everlasting duration.
Saturitas can mean abundance or plenty. The entry cites the full barns of Proverbs 3:10.
Sermo can denote a single saying or expression as well as a conversation or discourse.
Si can introduce an indirect inquiry or expression of doubt.
Simulacrum denotes a likeness or representation. The examples include statues of gods.
The preposition sine governs the ablative and expresses absence.
Sors can denote a lot that is cast, an allotted share or task, or one’s destiny.
Species can denote outward appearance or beauty.
Spiritus includes breath and the human spirit or mind. The entry also records Spiritus Sanctus.
Spiro can describe breathing. The entry gives the perfect spiravi and the supine spiratum.
Sponsa, treated under spondeo, denotes a betrothed woman or bride.
Stimulus can denote a goad or a sting and, figuratively, an incentive.
Suggero can mean to supply something or bring it to someone’s mind.
Summus is treated under superus as its superlative and can designate what is highest.
Supplico is a first-conjugation verb of humble entreaty, with the perfect in -āvi and the supine in -ātum.
Suscito can mean to awaken a sleeper or raise the dead.
Teneo can mean to hold, keep, maintain, or restrain.
The noun testis can refer to a witness, including an eyewitness.
Transeo can mean to cross or pass along a route and, figuratively, to pass away or pass something over.
Transfero can mean to carry across, transcribe, translate, or transform.
Tribulus, a masculine second-declension noun, can denote a thorn-bearing plant or a caltrop.
Tuba, genitive tubae, denotes a trumpet.
Tympanum denotes a percussion instrument such as a drum or timbrel.
In direct questions ubi asks where. These uses are grouped in section I.B.
Veneror is deponent and means to revere or venerate. The entry also records an active form.
The adverb vero, treated under verus, can mark an affirmation, a contrast, or a transition.
The noun victōrĭa has a short i before the ending.
Virga can denote a green shoot, a twig, or a rod.
Britt marks Cherub indeclinable and identifies Cherubim as the Hebrew plural. The abbreviation is explained on p. xxxvi.
Britt gives both genitive and dative government. He illustrates the dative from the Mass and litanies.
Britt records spero in the sense of trusting, with in followed by the ablative or the accusative.
The Vulgate uses Deus as the vocative as well as the nominative.
Dies is a fifth-declension noun, usually masculine. The feminine singular is especially common for a fixed date.
The defective verb has the request forms quaeso and quaesumus. The note records occasional further forms in early Latin.
Deponent verbs have passive forms with active or reflexive meaning. Their gerundive has passive meaning.
Genesis identifies Abel as a shepherd. He brings an offering from his flock, and the Lord looks favourably upon him and his offering.
